name: Apollo 11 Lunar Module (Descent Stage)
confidence: Confirmed site (landing site coordinates; imaged by LRO)
beginning: Apollo 11 was sent to meet a national goal: land humans on the Moon and return them safely. The Lunar Module 'Eagle' was built for one job, to carry two astronauts down to the surface and back up again.
mission_story: On 20 July 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed Eagle at Tranquility Base. They spent about 21 hours on the surface, deployed experiments and collected lunar samples.
legacy: The descent stage served as the launch platform for the ascent stage and was left behind to save weight. It still marks the place where humanity first touched the Moon, and NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has photographed it from orbit.
scientific_value: It is the physical record of the first crewed lunar landing and a protected-heritage candidate for future lunar missions.

name: Apollo 11 Laser Retroreflector
confidence: Confirmed site (deployed near the Apollo 11 landing site; map pin is the site, not the exact spot)
beginning: Scientists wanted a precise way to measure the distance between Earth and the Moon. A passive array of mirrors that reflects laser light straight back to its source needs no power and no maintenance.
mission_story: Aldrin and Armstrong set up the array on the surface in July 1969. Observatories on Earth fire laser pulses at it and time how long the light takes to return.
legacy: Unlike most left-behind hardware, the retroreflector is not retired. It has supported lunar ranging measurements for decades and is a rare abandoned object that is still doing science.
scientific_value: Lunar laser ranging measures the Earth-Moon distance very precisely and supports tests of gravity and studies of the Moon's interior.

name: Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle
confidence: Confirmed site (Apollo 15 landing area; rover parked near the Lunar Module)
beginning: Earlier Apollo crews could only explore on foot, close to the lander. Apollo 15 introduced the Lunar Roving Vehicle so astronauts could travel farther and carry more tools and samples.
mission_story: David Scott and James Irwin drove the folding electric rover across the Hadley-Apennine region in July-August 1971, reaching sites that would have been out of walking range.
legacy: The rover was parked near the Lunar Module and left on the Moon because bringing it home was not possible within the mission's weight limits. It remains there today.
scientific_value: It proved that vehicles can greatly extend human surface exploration and informed later rover designs.

name: Perseverance Parachute
confidence: APPROXIMATE (placed near the landing site; exact position not used)
beginning: Landing a car-sized rover on Mars is hard because the thin atmosphere gives little braking. Mars 2020 used a supersonic parachute as one stage of its entry, descent and landing sequence.
mission_story: The parachute deployed during Perseverance's descent on 18 February 2021 and slowed the spacecraft before the rover was lowered to the surface.
legacy: Once its job was done, the parachute was released and landed on the Martian surface. It has since been seen in images taken from orbit and from the surface.
scientific_value: Data from the descent helps engineers design safer landings for future, heavier Mars missions.

name: Perseverance Backshell
confidence: APPROXIMATE (placed near the landing site; exact position not used)
beginning: During the trip to Mars and the fall through its atmosphere, the rover was protected inside an aeroshell. The backshell was the upper half that stayed attached to the parachute.
mission_story: The backshell shielded the rover from the cold of space and the stress of descent, then separated so the descent stage could fly the rover to a gentle touchdown.
legacy: It was released and came down on the Martian surface a short distance from the rover. NASA has published photographs of the debris.
scientific_value: Studying how landing hardware performed and where it came to rest helps validate entry, descent and landing models.
